citations.quote: In this chapter, the authors outline an approach to formally model verification strategies using Systems Modeling Language (SysML) in a way that enables the automatic generation of the corresponding Bayesian network. The approach includes the development of a verification metamodel that can be represented as a SysML profile. A notional example is included, in which a CubeSat verification strategy is produced in accordance with the SysML profile and a representative Bayesian network is created. Results from the Bayesian update are presented, and the impact on the SysML model is discussed.

Traditionally, all these artifacts are generated or controlled by a combination of independent or stand-alone documents. As with other document-based approaches in systems engineering [7], a document-based approach to verification planning generates several problems [6,8], including information inconsistencies (due to multiple information sources and recurring updates and task repetitions), wasted effort in manually typing and transferring information across information sources, difficulty in identifying and controlling change propagation, and loss of a holistic view of the verification enterprise.

By connecting verification strategy models with other engineering artifacts within a model-based systems engineering (MBSE) environment or, more generally, by leveraging digital engineering (DE), we anticipate significant impacts on velocity and deployed capabilities by reducing the time needed to complete verification activities (since documentation efforts can be automated directly from the model), improving consistency in the design and development process (since information points to single sources of truth), improving the holistic evaluation of the verification enterprise (engineering teams that include design engineers, verification managers, and integration and test engineers work concurrently in shared models), and enabling the use of quantitative methods to compute the confidence in the correct state of the system of interest.

Verification strategies, and the evidence collected through them, will be modeled using Bayesian networks [10]. Both models (of planning and of evidence) will be connected through SysML models of the system design.

In this way, given a prior confidence on the state of any of the system parameters (for example, $ \theta_{1} $ or $ \theta_{2} $ ), the confidence is updated using the Bayesian rule [27] as per the evidence gathered when executing related verification activities (for example, $ \nu_{1} $ or $ \nu_{2} $ ).

In this work, a preliminary system verification metamodel has been produced. This is based on the "information model" presented in the work by Salado [6]. Other existing metamodels will be considered as we develop the metamodel.

In this task, we create a new SysML profile to model verification artifacts. We will employ activity diagrams to model the verification plan. Activity nodes will be used to model activities related to verification (e.g., the performance of an analysis, the conduction of a test, the preparation of an inspection, or the evaluation of test results). Information elements flowing between the activities will be used to capture the inputs and outputs of such activities (e.g., test configurations, test requirements, or test results).

In this task, we extend the profile developed in task 1 to enable the connection of systems models with verification models. The key idea of this task is that the definition of verification elements, such as test configurations, can be established by directly pointing to the systems model instead of creating them manually.

As stated in Sect. 3.1, the model-based approach incorporates SysML activity diagrams to model the verification plan. The system's logical architecture is modeled using SysML block definition diagrams and internal block diagrams. The system's functionality is captured using SysML activity diagrams. Requirements are captured using SysML requirement diagrams and traceability will be established from the requirements, through the system's logical and functional architectures to the verification activities.

The preliminary metamodel for this work is defined in Fig. 3, has been adapted from the study by Salado [6], and has been reproduced as a SysML profile. This profile then ensures that the systems model, produced using SysML, corresponds to the metamodel. Concepts are modeled as either SysML classes or SysML activities and the relations between them as SysML association relations.

In this section, the preliminary metamodel presented in Sect. 4 is applied to a notional CubeSat design [32]. The system requirements, architecture, and functionality are represented using SysML. The verification strategy and activities are also represented using SysML. These two aspects are connected in accordance with the preliminary metamodel, as captured in the SysML profile. A representative Bayesian network, to be generated by the SysML model, is also presented.

Once the status of the verification strategy has been updated in the Bayesian model and the confidence values have been calculated, these values are to be automatically stored in the SysML model as value properties. These values may be used to inform future decisions regarding the verification strategy (i.e., whether further verification activities are required). In this way, the verification strategy itself can be simulated.

The measurement value (1.34 kg) has been stored in the SysML model, and a SysML <<trace>> relationship has been defined to provide traceability between this value and the relevant <<VerificationActivity>>. The 91.1% confidence value calculated by the Bayesian model is automatically stored in the SysML model.

Following the completion of the «VerificationActivity》“Perform System Mass Analysis,” the system mass is estimated to be 9.68 kg and there is 80.3% confidence that the actual CubeSat will pass the system mass requirement. The «VerificationActivity》“Weigh Prototype” is then completed, and this also results in a mass estimate that is less than the upper limit of 10 kg (9.74 kg). This increases the confidence that the actual system mass will pass the mass requirement (from 80.3% to 86.9%).

Note that in this case study, the Bayesian network comprises relatively simple probability distributions. For example, if the measurement of the mass of the virtual prototype of a subsystem passes the relevant mass requirement, then the resulting confidence that the actual subsystem will pass the mass requirement is 91.1%. It is also possible to define more complex probability distributions.

An example has been presented in which a verification strategy for a notional CubeSat was captured using a SysML profile based on a preliminary verification metamodel. A representative Bayesian network was produced, based on mathematical models of verification patterns published in previous works. The results from the Bayesian network were captured in the SysML model as the verification strategy was undertaken.

Next steps will include further development of the metamodel, including the incorporation of other published works on metamodels and ontologies regarding systems verification. We will also develop a plug-in to automatically generate the corresponding Bayesian network from the SysML model and return the resulting confidence values back to the SysML model. This approach will be tested on more comprehensive case studies and compared to a traditional document-based approach.
